title: First M5 Pro baseline run (Tier A models)
description:
Tier A calibration models: Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B at int4, 4096-token prompts. Small enough to run on all three machines, which is what makes cross-machine comparison valid.

Use the mlx_transformers_benchmark methodology specifically, NOT oMLX or another harness. Published M5 Max figures for these exact models are 2,785 and 1,740 tok/s prefill, and only same-harness comparisons are meaningful. Cross-harness numbers disagree wildly: oMLX reports an M5 Pro at 466 tok/s prefill on a 27B while mlx_transformers_benchmark reports an M5 Max at 476 tok/s on a comparable 27B, which would imply zero speedup and is obviously an artifact.

Hygiene: three repetitions, report the median, plugged in, other apps closed, runtime version pinned, thermal state logged.
notes: Partial: 3-rep ollama_cask qwen3.5:4b Metal calibration + concurrency ladder (n=1..25) recorded in workstation/ai/bench/results/. Still needed to close: qwen3.5:9b pull, mlx_lm.server path, mlx_transformers_benchmark for published 2785/1740 comparison. Do not pin Ollama (lib-ldz) until that exists.

title: Add ollama-app cask to workstation
description:
Repo: imkarrer/workstation. File: darwin/homebrew.nix.

Add "ollama-app" to the casks list. This IS a nix-darwin-managed install because nix-homebrew is already enabled in flake.nix, so it stays declarative and in git.

Cask token is `ollama-app` (former token: `ollama`), requires macOS 14+. It symlinks /opt/homebrew/bin/ollama into /Applications/Ollama.app/Contents/Resources/ollama, so the CLI lands on PATH for free.

CRITICAL: do NOT install the Homebrew `ollama` FORMULA or nixpkgs `pkgs.ollama`. Homebrew issue #285982 documents the formula bottle shipping the MLX runner but omitting llama-server, so GGUF and embedding models fail. If the formula is present alongside the cask it wins the /opt/homebrew/bin/ollama symlink and brew only warns 'skipping link', leaving you silently on the broken binary.

Follows the repo's existing placement rule: .app bundles go in homebrew.nix as casks, like google-chrome.

title: Calibrate against published M5 Max figures
description:
Compare the b4 Tier A results against published mlx_transformers_benchmark M5 Max numbers (Qwen3.5-4B: 2,785 tok/s prefill; Qwen3.5-9B: 1,740 tok/s) to derive the EMPIRICAL scaling factor rather than trusting the theoretical one.

Expected: near 2.0x decode, 2.0-2.5x prefill. If measurement disagrees with theory, measurement wins and the plan's capacity estimates get revised.

This factor then projects every other measurement onto the Mac Studio.

title: Escalation protocol for student disclosures
description:
THE MOST IMPORTANT NON-TECHNICAL ITEM IN THE PLAN. Must be complete before any student touches the system.

Middle schoolers will disclose things to a chatbot they will not say to an adult. The system needs a defined path for self-harm, abuse, and bullying disclosures that routes to the school counselor, not just a refusal message.

Define: what triggers escalation, who reviews the flag queue and on what cadence, how fast a human sees it, what gets retained and for how long (this is the exception to the 30-45 day purge), and what the student sees in the moment.

Build this BEFORE students touch it, not after.

title: Epic C: Hardware validation
description: Gate the ~$5,400 purchase on measurement rather than extrapolation. Neither available machine is an M5 Max, but the M5 Pro (right microarchitecture, wrong memory) and a rented M4 Max (right memory and core count, wrong microarchitecture) bracket it on both axes.

title: Publish the M5 Max projection
description:
Combine c2 and c3 into one defensible projection.

From the M4 Max results: scale prefill up roughly 3.5-4x for the M5 Neural Accelerators (same 40 GPU cores, so the gain is nearly all from the new matrix hardware) and decode 1.12-1.25x for bandwidth (546 to 614 GB/s). The M5 Pro results independently confirm the M5-generation prefill multiplier is real on this specific workload.

Must answer: how many concurrent students can one Mac Studio actually serve, and does the 128GB-over-64GB argument hold up? Full residency is estimated at ~101GB (35B-A3B 23GB + gpt-oss-120b 66GB + Llama Guard 4 8GB + embeddings 2GB + Parakeet 2GB), which does not fit in 64GB.

title: Epic E: School program
description: Non-technical, fully parallel, and should START IMMEDIATELY. DPI consultation and board scheduling have long lead times that the technical work does not, and e2 gates the purchase decision.

title: Board brief and budget
description:
One-page administrative ask with line-item budget for both the 128GB and 64GB builds, the Common School Fund eligibility argument, and WUFAR coding.

Year one total roughly $9,300-11,000: Mac Studio $5,400, AppleCare+ ~$380, external TB5 NVMe ~$400, Time Machine drive ~$300, UPS ~$200, locking enclosure ~$150, software $0 (all open source), setup stipend $1,500-3,000, staff PD ~$1,000. Ongoing is about $60/year in electricity plus 2-4 hours/week of librarian time.

A 64GB build with no stipend lands near $6,500 and is a legitimate pilot if the board balks.

Gates the purchase decision (c6).

title: DPI consultation on Common School Fund eligibility
description:
Wis. Stat. 43.70(3) permits Common School Fund (Library Aid) dollars for 'school library computers and related software' under three conditions, all of which this design meets:
  - The school board consults the district's licensed library media specialist (PI 8.01(2)(h))
  - The computers are HOUSED IN THE SCHOOL LIBRARY, which the Mac Studio form factor makes literal (a rack server in the district datacenter would NOT qualify)
  - Purchases align with the district's written long-range library plan

Coded to WUFAR Function 222000, Project Code 031.

Contact: Monica Treptow, DPI School Library Education Consultant, monica.treptow@dpi.wi.gov. Do this before ordering.

title: Purchase decision
description:
Recommended build: Mac Studio M5 Max, 18-core CPU / 40-core GPU, 128GB unified memory, 1TB internal SSD = $5,400 (roughly $5,000-5,200 at Apple education institutional pricing).

Skip the 8TB internal SSD: it costs $3,800 and buys nothing a ~$350 external Thunderbolt 5 NVMe will not. Max the memory instead, since it is soldered and unupgradeable on a 5-7 year school asset.

CTO ladder for reference: 40-core GPU base with 48GB is $3,100; 64GB is +$400; 128GB is +$2,000; SSD 1TB +$300, 8TB +$3,800.

Timing risk: pre-orders opened Aug 25, units ship Sept 22, and the memory supply crunch is what doubled the 128GB upgrade price versus M4 Max. If board approval slips past the ship date, consider ordering early and validating after.

Gated on c4 (projection), c5 (quality), e2 (board approval).

title: Verification script: confirm MLX is actually active
description:
Repo: imkarrer/workstation.

Every failure mode in this stack is a SILENT fallback rather than an error, so this check is load-bearing for every benchmark that follows.

Assert:
  1. `which ollama` resolves into /Applications/Ollama.app/... (not a formula or nix store path)
  2. Server logs report the MLX backend, not `library=metal` or `library=cpu`
  3. The MLX dylibs are arm64 (Ollama 0.20.4 shipped x86_64-only libmlxc.dylib / libmlx.dylib that failed to load on arm64 entirely; see ollama issue #15433)
  4. macOS is 26+ so the M5-optimized mlx_metal_v4 variant is selected rather than mlx_metal_v3

Ollama 0.12.9 also shipped a regression that silently fell back GPU-to-CPU, taking users from 53 tok/s to 7. This script is the guard against shipping a benchmark run on the wrong backend.
close_reason: Verification script in ai/verify-mlx.sh; MLX v4 loaded, no CPU fallback, formula absent.

comments.author: Isaac Karrer
comments.text: ai/verify-mlx.sh passes: realpath into Ollama.app, mlx_metal_v4 arm64 dylibs mapped into ollama serve, macOS 26.5.1. qwen3.5:4b is Q4_K_M GGUF so the child runner is llama-server/Metal at 100% GPU; parent still has mlx_metal_v4 loaded for MLX-format models. Script warns (does not fail) on that split so benchmark rows can record the runner.

title: Quality preflight: gpt-oss-120b via hosted API
description:
No technical blockers. START EARLY, this is on the critical path to the purchase decision.

DO NOT let the librarian judge answer quality on the 24GB laptop. A 12B model will underwhelm on readers' advisory, someone concludes local AI is not good enough, and a false negative kills the project.

Instead: gpt-oss-120b is open-weight and available on hosted APIs. Run the librarian's golden question set against it via API. Those questions are about books and contain no student PII. Then run the IDENTICAL weights locally in production. Quality gets settled before a dollar is spent, without sending student data anywhere.

Depends on having the golden question set from the librarian, which is an Epic E conversation.

Use the [services] block for long-running processes so `flox activate` starts them and exit stops them, which is the right lifecycle on a laptop; the same manifests run under launchd on the Mac Studio later.

Structure ai/ so it can be lifted out with `git subtree split` when the hardware arrives.

title: Local LLM client in the base flox env
description:
Repo: imkarrer/workstation. File: flox/.flox/env/manifest.toml.

Goal: use the model for real everyday work, not just benchmarks. `ollama run` already works in any shell via the cask symlink; what the base env adds is a one-shot client that pipes well, sitting alongside git and jq as 'interactive CLI userland'.

Add [profile] shell helpers rather than global env vars, e.g.:
  ask()  { ollama run "${LOCAL_MODEL:-qwen3.5:4b}" "$*"; }
  sumz() { ollama run "${LOCAL_MODEL:-qwen3.5:4b}" "Summarize concisely:\n\n$(cat)"; }

DO NOT set OPENAI_BASE_URL in [vars]. It is the tempting one-liner but silently redirects every OpenAI-compatible tool in every shell at the local model, and claude / claude-code are already installed on this machine.

Keep python, mlx-lm, and pymarc OUT of this env: it auto-activates in every shell. Those belong in ai/.flox (see a5).

Pull models: gpt-oss-20b (14GB, strong tool calling, doubles as the MoE performance proxy) and qwen3.5:4b (instant responses).

title: Rent an AWS EC2 M4 Max Mac instance
description:
M5 Max is NOT rentable and will not be before the purchase decision. Hosting providers buy Apple hardware through retail channels, so it typically reaches their fleets months after the Sept 22 ship date, realistically 2027. MacStadium, Scaleway, and AWS all top out at M4 today.

AWS EC2 offers an M4 Max Mac instance built on the M4 Max Mac Studio: 16-core CPU, 40-core GPU, 128GB unified memory. Same GPU core count and same memory as the target machine. Per-second billing with a 24-hour minimum on a dedicated host, so tens of dollars against a $5,400 decision.

Run what the laptop cannot: Tier B models (gpt-oss-120b at 66GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), full model residency, and the 25-concurrent-user ladder against the real lineup.

title: Compliance packet
description:
Privacy impact assessment using DPI's mini-template, data retention policy (30-45 day auto-purge with a flagged-event exception), and an AUP insert adopting DPI's AI Use Tiers (Human-Only / AI-Assist / AI-Optional) plus a student disclosure box.

Legal framing to get right:
  - Wis. Stat. 43.30 (library record confidentiality) governs PUBLIC libraries, not school libraries. Commonly conflated; get it right in the board memo.
  - FERPA and Wis. Stat. 118.125 (pupil records) are the operative rules. Chat logs tied to a student identity are plausibly pupil records, bringing parent inspection rights and a 60-day response window. Short retention plus written policy is the mitigation.
  - COPPA regulates commercial operators. A school-hosted non-commercial system is not a covered operator, which is a real structural advantage over ChatGPT or Gemini in a building full of 11-to-13-year-olds.
  - DPI's tool-vetting checklist asks whether the vendor signs a DPA, whether student data trains models, and whether data is deleted at contract end. With no vendor, all three are satisfied by construction.

REPO IS PUBLIC. Commit the template and the legal reasoning here, since a board member or another district being able to read it is a feature. The FILLED-IN assessment — real staff names, real systems, real network detail — goes in a district-controlled private location, not in git.

title: Confirm the laptop's GPU tier
description:
M5 Pro ships as either 15-core CPU / 16-core GPU or 18-core CPU / 20-core GPU, both at 307GB/s. 24GB is the base config, which suggests the 16-core variant.

This sets the prefill scaling ratio to the 40-core M5 Max: 16 cores gives 2.5x, 20 cores gives 2.0x. Decode scales with bandwidth either way, 307 to 614 GB/s = exactly 2.0x.

Check with: system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType

title: Safety pipeline and flag queue
description:
Two-stage gate: Llama Prompt Guard 2 (22M, fast first-pass jailbreak detector) in front of Llama Guard 4 12B (input and output content classification, custom categories tuned for grades 6-8). Both run locally.

Note these are complementary, not redundant: Llama Guard 4 is a content classifier and NOT a prompt-injection detector, so stacking with Prompt Guard 2 covers both axes.

System prompts enforce RAG-grounded citations by default. Plus a librarian-reviewable flag queue wired to the e4 escalation protocol.

title: Benchmark workloads
description:
Repo: imkarrer/workstation, path ai/bench/workloads/.

  - prefill_sweep : 512 / 1k / 2k / 4k / 8k / 16k prompt tokens
  - rag_realistic : real MARC-shaped chunks plus librarian questions, ~6k tokens
  - concurrency   : N = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 25

Also measure prefix-cache benefit (identical system prompt repeated vs unique prompts) and thermal drift (same workload for ten minutes, first-minute vs last-minute delta).

The prefix-cache number matters most: the plan predicts caching the ~1500-token system prompt plus cutting retrieval from 8 chunks to 4 drops per-query prefill cost roughly 60%, which is what makes a class of 25 viable.

title: Flox agent-skills plugin (not a [skills] table)
description:
Design and prototype a first-class [skills] table for Flox manifests so project agent skills live in the environment instead of .claude/skills / .cursor/skills copies.

Why: Flox already says clone + activate is setup. That is false for the coding agent. A [skills] section is the [services] analogue for Agent Skills (SKILL.md), projected into .agents/skills on activate.

Does not violate Flox architecture if: local src= is first-class (not catalog-only), projection is generated+gitignored, harness detection uses installed dirs / the portable .agents bus rather than the current IDE process.

Proof path: convention prototype in this repo (beads skill), scanner that would feed floxify, then a product ticket under flox/product#1209 / #1240. Rust CLI / flox-manifest schema last.
design:
Proposal: package first, schema later.

Pitch to Flox is a plugin package (etc/profile.d + [plugins.flox-agent-skills]), not a [skills] table. Promote only after adoption (floxify always emits it, include-merge, discovery CLI, working-tree contract).

Repo:
- Proof: in-tree in library-ai-lab (.flox/pkgs or [hook]). No second GitHub repo.
- Share / real pkg-path: dedicated public repo + flox publish → `flox install owner/flox-agent-skills`. Lab stays first consumer.
- Flox may later take it into their catalog.

UX: plugin does not install skills.
1. Enable once: flox install owner/flox-agent-skills (or floxify).
2. Local skill: drop .flox/skills/<name>/SKILL.md; plugin auto-discovers on activate.
3. Catalog skill: flox install owner/some-skill (package drops share/skills); same projection.
4. Import: optional `flox-agent-skills import` copies .claude/.cursor skills into .flox/skills.
5. There is no `flox skills install` until a schema promotion.

Plugin scans .flox/skills/* and $FLOX_ENV/share/skills/*; [plugins] only holds targets. Dev mode only. .agents/skills gitignored.
acceptance_criteria:
- Written design: why [skills] vs [plugins] vs share/skills-on-[install]
- Prototype: activate projects at least the beads skill into .agents/skills from a declared source
- Scanner: inventories project-local harness skill dirs and emits a [skills] table (dry-run on library-ai-lab + workstation)
- floxify notes: scan list, dedup, skip user-global and skills-cursor
- No Flox CLI fork required for the prototype
notes:
End-to-end example locked to mattpocock/skills (tdd, code-review, grill-with-docs).

Today: npx skills add copies into .agents/.cursor/.claude. Claude plugin is subscribe/read-only.

Flox story A (editable): flox install projector; import Matt’s dirs into .flox/skills; activate symlinks .agents/skills. Same philosophy as skills.sh.

Flox story B (subscribe): flox install projector + flox install mattpocock-skills catalog package. Same philosophy as Claude plugin.

Story C: catalog set + local override of one skill by name.

Proof: in-lab copy of tdd into .flox/skills + hook projector. No second repo until we want a pkg-path.

title: AI literacy curriculum unit
description:
Runs alongside Phase 2 supervised student access.

Make RAG-grounded mode with visible citations the DEFAULT rather than an option, with persistent 'this can be wrong, check the source' framing in the UI. For a middle school this is simultaneously a safety control and the curriculum.

Be honest about the capability envelope in the teaching material: readers' advisory and catalog search are at parity with frontier models because they are retrieval-grounded; transcription actually beats cloud Whisper (Parakeet v3 at 6.32% English WER vs 7.83%); research help has a modest gap; multi-step math has a real gap and this should not be presented as a math tutor.

title: Dogfood review after two weeks of real use
description:
Use the local model as a genuine daily driver for two weeks, then write up what broke, what was missing, and which model handled which task well.

This is the cheapest quality signal available. A configuration that survives real daily use is worth far more as a school template than one that only passes a demo, and problems surface here that no benchmark will find.

Output: workstation/ai/docs/dogfood-notes.md

comments.author: Isaac Karrer
comments.text: Daily-driver POC accepted 2026-08-27. Dogfood clock starts now: use ask/sumz and qwen3.5:4b (and gpt-oss:20b when quality matters) for real work. Write-up due ~2026-09-10 at workstation/ai/docs/dogfood-notes.md.

title: Epic D: Library system
description: The actual application: catalog RAG, chat interface, safety pipeline. Mostly buildable on the laptop; only production deployment is gated on hardware.

title: Network isolation and the library darwinConfiguration
description:
The privacy firewall, in order of how convincing each control is to a school board:

1. Default-deny outbound at the firewall. The Mac Studio's VLAN gets no egress. Model downloads and macOS updates happen in a scheduled maintenance window with a temporary allowlist. Auditable, reversible, and demonstrable in a board meeting.
2. Catalog indexed, circulation data never touched (see d1).
3. No API keys anywhere on the box, so no accidental fallback path.

Second darwinConfiguration 'library' sharing common modules with 'dev', but with the lockdown, iogpu.wired_limit_mb around 118000, and OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 rather than 30m.

Use upstream Nix, NEVER Determinate: flox does not support it. This is already the documented rule in the workstation repo.

title: Chat UI, auth, RBAC, retention purge
description:
Open WebUI: single container, native Ollama integration, built-in RAG with hybrid search and reranking, RBAC scoped to knowledge bases, OIDC/SAML, audit logging as a native stack.

License caveat: removing Open WebUI branding requires 50-or-fewer users per rolling 30 days or a paid agreement. Using it at any scale is fine; white-labeling it is not. If branding it as the school's own tool matters for the AI-literacy goal, LibreChat is MIT with no such clause, at the cost of running MongoDB and Meilisearch alongside.

Container runtime: Colima or Podman, NOT Docker Desktop, which requires a paid subscription above 250 employees and many districts exceed that.

Auth via OIDC against whatever the district already runs. Retention purge at 30-45 days.

title: Pin the Ollama version via in-repo cask
description:
Repo: imkarrer/workstation. New: Casks/ollama-pinned.rb.

Casks track latest, which is wrong for a benchmark baseline and risky given Ollama's history (0.12.9 silent GPU-to-CPU fallback; 0.20.4 broken arm64 MLX dylibs).

The repo already has the machinery: Casks/ is a trusted in-repo tap with clone_target pointing at the local checkout, and dr-sprinto is already installed that way. Write a cask with a fixed version and sha256.

Gotcha from the repo README: after bumping an in-repo cask, run `brew untap imkarrer/casks` before darwin-switch, because brew bundle will not re-clone an already-installed tap.

Do this AFTER a baseline exists so you know which version you are pinning to.

comments.author: Isaac Karrer
comments.text: Still correctly blocked on the first M5 Pro baseline (lib-3tm). Do not pin until that run exists.

title: Production provisioning and runbook
description:
Rebuild-from-scratch bootstrap sequence, Caddy TLS, sops-nix secrets for the OIDC client secret, and an explicit list of state deliberately NOT in git: model weights (pin by SHA256 in models.lock.json plus a fetch script), chat logs, the vector index (regenerable), macOS/FileVault/MDM enrollment.

Must include a non-Nix escape hatch — plain Homebrew plus shell scripts — so hitting a Nix wall can never be the reason the project dies. Nix solves reproducibility and introduces a knowledge dependency; the runbook has to address both.

title: MARC ingest pipeline
description:
Parse a Destiny 'Catalog > Export Titles' MARC file with pymarc, chunk and embed BIBLIOGRAPHIC RECORDS ONLY, load into the vector store.

This is the privacy firewall, expressed as architecture: the pipeline never touches patron records, checkout history, or fines. Books are indexed; who read them is not. Destiny has no bulk-MARC REST API, so this is a scheduled export plus a parse rather than a live integration, which is a feature since the boundary is enforced by the export format itself.

Document the refresh schedule and the explicit exclusion of all patron and circulation data.

title: Retrieval quality tuning
description:
Chunking strategy and retrieval tuning for readers' advisory and catalog search.

This is where most of the actual value lives and it is MODEL-INDEPENDENT, so it can be perfected on the laptop. For these tasks the quality ceiling is set by how well MARC records are chunked, not by model size. The ingest pipeline is the bottleneck, not the model.

Target top-4 retrieval rather than top-8, since halving retrieved context is half of the concurrency fix.

title: Draft Flox product note: plugin vs [skills] promotion
description: After the prototype, draft a note as a child of flox/product#1209: inbound project skills belong on the 1.14 [plugins] valve; [skills] is a promotion if floxify always writes it. Distinct from #1240 (outbound Flox skills on FloxHub). Do not open a schema RFC unless asked.

title: BaseRT adapter (timeboxed research)
description:
Repo: imkarrer/workstation, path ai/bench/runtimes/basert.py.

BaseRT (arxiv 2607.19438, github.com/basecompute/baseRT) is an inference engine with hand-written Metal tensor-core kernels reporting up to 3.9x higher prefill than mlx-lm on M5 Pro, including 2.2-3.9x on the MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B.

Prefill is precisely what caps concurrency in the class-of-25 scenario, so a win of that magnitude would change the capacity math outright. Treat as research, not a dependency. Timebox it.
